carousels.title: The 95-5 Rule: 95% of your market can't buy today
carousels.caption:
95% of your market can't buy from you today.

That's not a bad quarter, it's the 95-5 rule. Research out of the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute for Marketing Science puts it plainly: at any given moment, only around 5% of B2B buyers in your category are actively in-market. The other 95% aren't ignoring your product. They're simply not buying anything, from anyone, right now.

Most demand gen budgets don't reflect that. Almost everything is built for the 5%: book-a-demo CTAs, bottom-funnel offers, retargeting the same warm accounts on repeat. Meanwhile the 95% who will eventually buy get nothing, because nothing is being said to them yet.

Here's the reframe: the 95% aren't lost pipeline. They're future pipeline. The job isn't to convert them this quarter, it's to be the name they remember when the need finally shows up. That's brand and category-memory work, and it compounds in a way a single demo CTA never will.

Then, when the 5% do raise a hand, you still need the fast, obvious next step: a clear offer, a fast reply, no friction.

Most teams run one play. The ones who win pipeline consistently run both: long-game category presence, and a sharp, immediate capture motion for the in-market few.

Which one is your budget actually built for right now?

carousels.title: The Dark Funnel, explained
carousels.caption:
Your best leads never touched your website first.

Here's what that actually looks like: a buyer drops a question into their peer Slack, "anyone used a tool like this?" A few people name you. The buyer goes to your site directly, already halfway convinced. Your analytics logs the visit as "direct traffic." What really happened was word of mouth, in a channel you can't see.

Marketers have started calling this the dark funnel: the research, recommendations, and conversations that shape a buying decision before it ever produces a trackable session. No UTM, no referrer, no record.

Why it matters: by the time a lead fills out a form, the decision has often already been made somewhere off-platform. Your attribution model is measuring the moment after the moment that mattered.

You can't track dark social. But you can earn it. Two things actually work:

Be the thing worth screenshotting: a sharp post, a genuinely useful tool, a founder point of view people want to forward to a colleague.

Show up in the rooms you can't measure: the communities, newsletters, podcasts, and peer circles where your buyers already talk shop, long before they ever open a search bar.

None of this shows up cleanly in a dashboard. It shows up in pipeline you can't fully explain, from accounts that arrived already sold.

Where is your category actually talking about you right now, and do you know?

carousels.title: The Decoy Effect: how a worse option makes people spend more
carousels.caption:
Adding a deliberately worse option can make people spend more. Used honestly, it is one of the most useful ideas in pricing and proposals.

It is called the decoy effect. You do not change your two real options. You add a third that is clearly weaker, and suddenly one of the originals looks like the obvious choice.

The classic case is The Economist. Three plans: web only at $59, print only at $125, and print plus web also at $125. Print-only looks pointless, and that is exactly the point. It exists to make the $125 bundle feel like a steal. In Dan Ariely's test, that single decoy moved the bundle from 32% to 84% of buyers.

Why it works: people are bad at judging value on its own, so we judge by comparison. A decoy hands the brain an easy, flattering comparison, and it takes it.

How to use it without being manipulative: in your pricing or your next proposal, place a deliberately weaker tier next to the one you actually want chosen. Do not sell the decoy. Frame with it. Three options, and the one you are steering toward becomes the obvious pick.

A worse option is not clutter. It is context. Give people something to compare against, and the choice you want makes itself.

Which of your offers could use a decoy next to it?
